terms.comment: Beauty of body, of things and of the mind: Cicero defines it as a fit shape of the limbs with a pleasing colour (Tusc. 4.31), and speaks of the beauty of virtue (Off. 2.37). Its two kinds, he says, are venustās, womanly grace, and dignitās, manly dignity (Off. 1.130).

evidence: Hor. Ep. 1.4.6: dī tibi fōrmam … dederant (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: First shape, form, a figure (see form); used alone, a fine form, beauty, above all of a person.

evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.4.5: signa eximiā venustāte (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Loveliness and grace, of people, of works of art and of wit and style; for Cicero the womanly kind of beauty (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: fōrma bonum fragile est, quantumque accēdit ad annōs fit minor, et spatiō carpitur ipsa suō
phrases.english: beauty is a fragile good: the more the years increase, the less it becomes, and it is worn away by its own span

phrases.latin: sī quis in caelum ascendisset nātūramque mundī et pulchritūdinem sīderum perspexisset, īnsuāvem illam admīrātiōnem eī fore
phrases.english: if a man went up to heaven and looked on the nature of the world and the beauty of the stars, the wonder of it would give him no joy

phrases.latin: Neque enim terrās tibi sed fōrmam aliquam ad eximiam pulchritūdinem pictam vidēberis cernere
phrases.english: for you will think you are looking not at land but at a picture painted to be supremely beautiful

sources: Lewis & Short: pulchritudo · Lewis & Short: forma · Lewis & Short: venustas
